lines.speaker: Protesilaus
lines.text: My lord, my king, our Zeus below — and you, daughter of Demeter — do not turn away a prayer born of love.
lines.note: Formal supplication; Protesilaus is playing every available card, divine and personal. Earnest, not grovelling.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: What exactly are you asking of us? And who are you?
lines.note: Pluto's default intake-desk tone: not unkind, but he needs the form filled out.

lines.speaker: Protesilaus
lines.text: I am Protesilaus, son of Iphicles, of Phylace — a comrade-in-arms of the Achaeans, and the first man to die before Troy. What I am asking is this: let me go up, just for a little while, and live again.
lines.note: The request is stated plainly. He knows it's a lot.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: That particular desire, Protesilaus, is the one desire every dead man shares. And not one of them has ever gotten it.
lines.note: Dry, not cruel. He has said this ten thousand times.

lines.speaker: Protesilaus
lines.text: It isn't life I'm asking for, Hades. It's my wife. I left her in the bridal chamber — still a new bride — and sailed away to war, and then had the miserable luck to be killed in the landing, by Hector. [pause] The longing for her is — it doesn't ease, my lord. I only want to see her, just for a moment, and then I'll come back down.
lines.note: Genuine; not performed. This is the collection's most emotionally honest petition. Let it breathe.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: Did you not drink from the Lethe, Protesilaus?

lines.speaker: Protesilaus
lines.text: I did, my lord. The feeling was simply... too large for it.
lines.note: Quiet. This is the best line in the dialogue. Don't oversell it.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: Then wait. She'll arrive eventually — and you won't even need to make the trip.
lines.note: Not heartless — it's a genuine practical solution. He's trying to help in his way.

lines.speaker: Protesilaus
lines.text: I cannot bear the wait, Pluto. You have loved someone yourself. You know what it is.
lines.note: A direct appeal to Pluto's own experience with Persephone. Calculated, but not cynical.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: And what exactly will one day above accomplish? You'll spend it grieving, and then you'll be right back here doing the same.
lines.note: Not dismissive — he is genuinely pointing out the flaw in the plan.

lines.speaker: Protesilaus
lines.text: I believe I can persuade her to follow me down. So instead of one dead soul, you'll have two, before long.
lines.note: Protesilaus plays his best card. Said with careful, quiet logic.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: That is not how this works, and it has never worked that way.
lines.note: Firm, but there's a slight hesitation under it — Persephone is listening.

lines.speaker: Protesilaus
lines.text: Let me remind you, Pluto: you gave Eurydice back to Orpheus for precisely this reason. And you sent my kinswoman Alcestis up with Heracles, as a favour to him. Precedent exists.
lines.note: He has done his research. The legal argument is made calmly, without triumph.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: But you'll be presenting yourself to that beautiful bride of yours as a bare, featureless skull. How is she even supposed to recognise you? She'll be frightened — I'm quite sure of it — she'll run, and you'll have made the journey for nothing.
lines.note: Pluto is not trying to win; he's flagging a real practical problem. He's already half-persuaded.

lines.speaker: Persephone
lines.text: Then solve that too, husband. Tell Hermes: once Protesilaus is back in the light, one touch of the staff — and make him a young man again, as handsome as he was when he left the bridal chamber.
lines.note: Persephone enters the scene and immediately solves the problem Pluto was dithering over. Quiet authority; no fuss. This is the closest the collection comes to an act of simple kindness.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: Since Persephone agrees — [pause] take him up. Make him a bridegroom again. And you — remember you have one day.
lines.note: Pluto's ruling. The pause before 'take him up' is where he makes his decision. Said to Hermes; the last sentence is to Protesilaus. The authority is absolute, and he wears it lightly.
